comment-block.comment: Opens at ## and closes at the NEXT ##, which takes the rest of its line with it. The closer must therefore match to end of line, or a line reading '## and then some' would leave the tail as code.
comment-block.name: comment.block.profi-c

comment-line.comment: A single mark. Placed after the block rule so that ## is never read as two of these.
comment-line.name: comment.line.number-sign.profi-c

block-string.comment: Three quotes to three quotes, holding nothing that is read. Offered before the ordinary string rule, or the first two quotes would close an empty one and leave the rest as code.
block-string.name: string.quoted.triple.profi-c

interpolation.comment: A hole holds ordinary code, so the whole grammar is offered inside it and a name, a call or a number reads there as it does anywhere. The braces themselves are marked as punctuation rather than as string, which is what tells a reader where the text stops. A format after the colon is not code and is left as part of the string.
interpolation.name: meta.interpolation.profi-c

patterns.comment: Everything from the colon to the closing braces. Matched before the rest so a pattern such as 'yyyy-MM-dd' is not read as subtraction.

fraction.comment: Matched before the plain number rule, or 22|7 reads as two integers around an operator.
fraction.name: constant.numeric.fraction.profi-c

end.comment: A closer names what it closes, so the pair reads as one thing rather than a keyword beside a noun.

declaration.comment: A word and the name after it, wherever that name can only be a type or a function. Each rule captures the word too, and so has to be offered before the plain keyword rules: a keyword matched on its own consumes itself, and the name beside it is then reached with nothing left to say what it is.

patterns.comment: Held apart from 'namespace' below so it can be coloured with 'function' and 'let': the words that introduce a thing which then holds something. A model, a structure, and an enumeration hold members; a function holds a body; a let holds a value. A namespace holds none of those — it only says where a name sits.

A namespace's own name is left plain. It names a place rather than a thing, and colouring it as a type made 'Tour.Shapes' read as though Shapes were declared inside a Tour. The whole dotted name is consumed here even though nothing is said about it, so that the qualifier rule below cannot take the first segment and leave the rest — which is what made these render half one colour and half another.
And the namespace a using names, for the same reason and by the same means.
What a model extends is a type and can be nothing else.
Without this the name after 'new' is followed by '(' and reads as a function call, which is the one place the grammar said something untrue rather than nothing.
A caught exception names its type before the name it binds.
Both type operators take a type on the right and nothing else.

qualified-type.comment: A type name with wherever it lives written in front of it. Only the last part names the type; the rest says where to look, and a place is not a thing. Reached through 'patterns' on a capture rather than as a rule of its own, so that every rule which already knows it is holding a type hands the whole run over and gets the split for free — and so that a namespace looks the same here as it does after 'namespace' and 'using', which colour nothing.

standard-namespace.comment: Standard is the namespace the language owns, not a type inside it. Consumed here, before the provided types and the qualifier rule below, so that neither takes it for one; whatever follows the dot is still coloured by whichever of them applies. Named alone among namespaces because it is the only one whose name the language knows — a program's own namespace in this position cannot be told from a type, and is left to the qualifier rule's guess.

typed-name.comment: A type standing in front of the name it describes, with no keyword to announce it: a field, a local, or a parameter. Offered after the primitive and provided types so those keep their own colour, and requiring a leading capital, which is convention rather than rule and so is the one thing here that can quietly miss.

patterns.comment: A parameter whose type is a primitive. The type has to be captured here rather than left for the rule that usually colours it: this match begins at the bracket or comma, one character earlier, and the engine takes whichever match starts first — so leaving the word alone would mean consuming it with nothing said about it.

qualifier.comment: A name with a dot after it: the type a global member is reached through, or the namespace a type is. Told from a value's member by the leading capital, which is convention rather than rule — a local named Total would be coloured as though it were a type. That is the cost of having no semantic model, and it is a smaller one than leaving every 'Program.Run()' and 'Circle.Pi' unlit.

patterns.comment: Words that say what something is or how far it reaches. Kept apart from the primitive types below: a reader telling a modifier from a type at a glance is worth more than the two matching.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.profi-c

patterns.comment: The same words, where no name follows: a lambda written 'function(a, b)', and 'let' anywhere.
patterns.name: keyword.declaration.profi-c

patterns.comment: Words that introduce or compose a declaration.
patterns.name: keyword.other.profi-c

patterns.comment: Spelled out rather than punctuated, which is the point of them.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.profi-c

type.comment: The primitive types, and the word that writes the type of a function. 'delegate' sits here rather than with the declaring words because that is what it does: it builds a type, as '[]' and '?' do, and never declares anything.
type.name: storage.type.profi-c

reserved-type.comment: Types the language provides. Not keywords, so the scanner reads them as ordinary names; they are listed here because a reader still meets them as part of the language.
reserved-type.name: support.class.profi-c

call.comment: A name with an argument list after it. Matched late, so a keyword is never taken for one.
